micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate a finite sum in sigma notation using the standard summation formulas and linearity
definitions: Sum_{i=m}^n f(i) = f(m)+f(m+1)+...+f(n); i is the index of summation (a dummy variable), m,n are the lower/upper limits.
Linearity: Sum_{i=m}^n (A f(i)+B g(i)) = A Sum f(i) + B Sum g(i) for constants A,B.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a sum of a linear combination of 1, i, and i^2 terms using Theorem 1 and linearity, expressing the result as a closed-form polynomial in n.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate Sum_{k=1}^n (6k^2-4k+3).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The summand is a polynomial in the index (constants, i, i^2 terms) — split via linearity and apply the three standard formulas (a),(b),(c) directly, term by term.
method_plan: Split the sum via linearity into separate sums of i^2, i, and 1
Apply the corresponding formula from Theorem 1 to each piece
Combine and simplify into a single polynomial in n
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct splitting via linearity
M1: correct application of each summation formula
A1: correctly simplified final polynomial in n

common_errors.description: Arithmetic error combining the resulting polynomial terms in n
Leaving the answer with n(n+1)(2n+1)/6-style factors unexpanded when a simplified polynomial was requested

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a finite geometric sum using formula (d), including sums that don't start with exponent 0.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate Sum_{i=1}^{10} 3*2^(i-1).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Each term is a constant times a fixed ratio raised to a power that increases by 1 each step (a geometric sequence) — signals formula (d) rather than the polynomial formulas.
method_plan: Identify the constant multiplier and the common ratio r
Match the sum to the form Sum r^(i-1) after factoring out the constant
Apply formula (d)
Simplify to a final numeric value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the constant factor and ratio r
M1: correct application of formula (d)
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Misapplying formula (d) when the exponent pattern does not actually start at r^0 for i=1
Arithmetic error evaluating r^n for larger n

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Set up and evaluate a sum from a word description (not already given in sigma notation), then apply the summation formulas.
question_archetypes.example: Find the sum of the squares of the first 20 odd positive integers.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The sum is described in words (e.g. 'sum of squares of the first n odd numbers') rather than already presented in sigma notation — the first step is translating the description into a sigma-notation sum before applying any formula.
method_plan: Translate the word description into a correct sigma-notation expression
Expand the summand if needed (e.g. expand (2k-1)^2) and split via linearity
Apply the summation formulas to each piece
Combine into a final numeric or closed-form answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct sigma-notation translation of the word description
M1: correct expansion and splitting via linearity
A1: correct final value after applying summation formulas

common_errors.description: Mistranslating the word description into the wrong summand or limits (e.g. using k instead of 2k-1 for odd numbers)
Expansion error squaring the binomial (2k-1)^2

micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize and evaluate a telescoping sum where consecutive terms cancel
definitions: A telescoping sum Sum_{i=m}^n [f(i+1)-f(i)] = f(n+1)-f(m), because consecutive terms cancel leaving only the first and last.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a sum already given in the form f(i+1)-f(i), recognizing the telescoping cancellation.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The summand is explicitly a difference of the same function evaluated at consecutive (or otherwise stepped) index values — a strong visual cue for telescoping rather than expanding and using Theorem 1.
method_plan: Identify the function f such that the summand is f(index+1)-f(index) (or similar)
Write out the first few and last few terms to see the cancellation pattern
Apply the telescoping formula to collapse to f(last)-f(first)
Evaluate the two remaining terms
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the telescoping structure
A1: correct collapse to the boundary terms
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Attempting to apply Theorem 1's polynomial formulas by expanding, missing the much faster telescoping cancellation
Off-by-one error in the boundary terms f(first) or f(last)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Show that a sum of the form 1/(j(j+1)) (or similar) telescopes after first decomposing the summand into a difference of two simpler fractions.
question_archetypes.answer: 1/(j(j+1)) = 1/j - 1/(j+1), so the sum telescopes to 1 - 1/(n+1) = n/(n+1)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The summand is a product of two consecutive linear factors in the denominator — a partial-fraction-style decomposition into 1/j - 1/(j+1) reveals hidden telescoping structure not obvious at first glance.
method_plan: Decompose the summand into a difference of two simpler terms (partial fractions)
Recognize the resulting sum telescopes
Collapse to the boundary terms and simplify
State the closed-form result
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct partial-fraction decomposition of the summand
M1: correct recognition and collapse of the telescoping sum
A1: correct simplified closed-form answer

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the telescoping structure is hidden until after decomposing the summand
Incorrect partial-fraction decomposition of 1/(j(j+1))

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Prove one of the standard summation formulas (e.g. Sum i^2) by constructing an appropriate telescoping identity and summing both sides.
question_archetypes.example: Prove Sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 by telescoping (k+1)^3-k^3=3k^2+3k+1.
question_archetypes.answer: Summing (k+1)^3-k^3 for k=1..n telescopes to (n+1)^3-1; equating to Sum(3k^2+3k+1) and solving for Sum k^2 using already-known Sum k and Sum 1 gives the formula.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to PROVE a summation formula, not just apply it — the standard technique is to expand a telescoping identity like (k+1)^3-k^3 and sum both sides, then solve algebraically for the unknown sum.
method_plan: Choose and expand an appropriate telescoping identity (e.g. (k+1)^3-k^3)
Sum both sides from k=1 to n, collapsing the left side via telescoping
Use already-established lower-order summation formulas (Sum k, Sum 1) to isolate the target sum
Solve algebraically for the desired closed form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct telescoping identity chosen and expanded
M1: correct summation and telescoping collapse of the left side
A1: correct use of lower-order formulas to isolate the target sum
A1: correct final proven formula

common_errors.description: Forgetting to use already-known lower order summation formulas, getting stuck solving for the target sum
Expansion error cubing (k+1)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Shift the index of summation or re-express a sum starting at a different index
definitions: Index shifting: Sum_{j=m}^{m+n} f(j) = Sum_{i=0}^n f(i+m) (substitute j=i+m); the index is always a dummy variable and never appears in the final answer.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Re-express a sum with nonstandard limits (not starting at i=1) as an equivalent sum starting at i=1, by substituting a shifted index.
question_archetypes.example: Express Sum_{j=3}^{17} sqrt(1+j^2) in the form Sum_{i=1}^n f(i).
question_archetypes.answer: Let j=i+2; sum becomes Sum_{i=1}^{15} sqrt(1+(i+2)^2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The sum's limits do not start at the standard i=1 (or i=0) — a substitution j=i+constant re-centers the limits without changing the value of the sum.
method_plan: Choose a substitution j = i + constant so the new index starts at the desired value
Determine the new upper limit by solving for i at the old upper limit
Substitute j=i+constant into the summand
Write the re-indexed sum with the new limits
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution chosen to shift the starting index
M1: correct new limits computed
A1: correct re-indexed summand and final expression

common_errors.description: Miscalculating the new upper (or lower) limit after the substitution
Forgetting the index is a dummy variable, and mistakenly leaving the old variable name (j) in the reindexed summand

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Combine two sums with different (but overlapping or adjacent) index ranges into a single sum, using index shifting to align them.
question_archetypes.example: Combine Sum_{i=1}^n a_i + Sum_{i=2}^{n+1} b_{i-1} into a single sum over i=1 to n.
question_archetypes.answer: Reindex the second sum with i=k-1 (so k=i+1 ranges 1 to n... adjust as needed): Sum_{i=1}^n (a_i+b_i) after correctly aligning indices
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two separate sums are given whose index ranges don't match, but they can be aligned into a single sum via reindexing one of them — common when combining Riemann-sum-like expressions.
method_plan: Identify the mismatch in index ranges between the two sums
Reindex one sum so its range matches the other's
Combine the two summands under a single sigma with linearity
Simplify the combined summand if possible
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct reindexing of one sum to align ranges
M1: correct combination under a single sigma
A1: correctly simplified final combined sum

common_errors.description: Combining the sums under a single sigma before the index ranges are actually aligned
Off-by-one error in the reindexing substitution

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a description or pattern of terms, express it correctly in sigma notation with a well-defined dummy index and correct limits (a prerequisite skill for later recognizing Riemann sums).
question_archetypes.example: Express the sum 1/2 + 2/3 + 3/4 + ... + 99/100 in sigma notation.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A pattern of terms is given informally (with '...') rather than already in sigma notation — identify the general term as a function of the position i and the correct starting/ending index.
method_plan: Identify the general pattern of the kth term as a function of k
Determine the correct starting and ending values of the index
Write the sum in sigma notation with the dummy variable never appearing in the final numeric answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct general term identified as a function of the index
A1: correct starting and ending limits
A1: correctly formatted sigma notation

common_errors.description: Misidentifying the general term's pattern (off-by-one in numerator or denominator)
Using an ambiguous or already-used variable name for the index

micro_skills.subtopic: Building and Evaluating S_n for Equal Subintervals
micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute the area under a curve from scratch by building S_n with equal subintervals and taking the limit as n->infinity
definitions: S_n = Sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i) Delta x_i approximates the area under y=f(x)>=0 on [a,b] using rectangles of height f(x_i) over each subinterval.
Area of R = lim (as n->infinity and max Delta x_i -> 0) S_n. For equal subintervals: Delta x = (b-a)/n, x_i = a + i*Delta x.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area under a linear function on [a,b] using the limit-of-sums definition with equal subintervals, and check against the elementary geometric area.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area under y=x+1 on [0,2] using the limit-of-sums definition.
question_archetypes.answer: S_n = 2(n+1)/n + 2 -> 4 as n->infinity (matches the trapezoid area 2*2+(1/2)*2*2=4)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem specifically instructs to use the LIMIT-OF-SUMS definition (not just 'find the area'), signaling the full S_n construction and limit must be shown, even though the answer could be found by elementary geometry.
method_plan: Set x_i = a + i*(b-a)/n and Delta x = (b-a)/n
Write S_n = Sum f(x_i) Delta x and expand f(x_i)
Apply the summation formulas (Theorem 1) to evaluate S_n in closed form
Take the limit as n->infinity
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct x_i and Delta x set up for equal subintervals
M1: correct S_n expressed and evaluated via summation formulas
A1: correct limit as n->infinity
A1: cross-check against elementary geometry if applicable

common_errors.description: Error simplifying S_n into a form where the n->infinity limit can be taken cleanly
Using f(x_{i-1}) inconsistently with the stated x_i choice

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area under y=x^2 (or a similar power function) on [0,b] with an unspecified endpoint parameter b, expressing the answer as a function of b.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area under y=x^2 on [0,b].
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The upper limit is a variable parameter b rather than a specific number — the final answer must be expressed as a function of b, previewing the Power Rule for antiderivatives.
method_plan: Set x_i = ib/n, Delta x = b/n
Write S_n = Sum (ib/n)^2 (b/n) and apply the i^2 summation formula
Simplify the resulting expression in n and b
Take the limit as n->infinity, leaving b as a parameter
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct x_i, Delta x setup with parameter b
M1: correct application of the i^2 summation formula
A1: correct limit taken, expressed as a function of b

common_errors.description: Losing track of the b-dependence while simplifying the n-dependent factors
Forgetting that only the n-dependent parts vanish in the limit; b must remain in the final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area under a shape whose height function is expressed relative to a general polynomial or shifted expression (not simply x^k), requiring more careful expansion of f(x_i) before applying the summation formulas.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area under y=(x+1)^2 on [0,3] using the limit-of-sums definition.
question_archetypes.answer: Expand f(x_i)=(x_i+1)^2 = x_i^2+2x_i+1 before summing; apply the i^2, i, and 1 formulas separately, then take the limit to get the exact area (evaluate numerically as needed)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is not simply x^k but a shifted or expanded expression — direct application of the i^2 formula alone is not enough; the expression must first be expanded into separate power-of-i terms.
method_plan: Set up x_i and Delta x for the equal-subinterval partition
Expand f(x_i) fully into separate power-of-i terms
Apply the relevant summation formula to each term separately, using linearity
Combine and take the limit as n->infinity
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct expansion of f(x_i) into separate power-of-i terms
M1: correct application of the summation formulas to each term
A1: correct combination and limit taken

common_errors.description: Expansion error in (x_i+1)^2 or similar binomial
Applying the i^2 summation formula directly to the unexpanded (x_i+1)^2 term, which is invalid

micro_skills.subtopic: Recognizing a Limit of a Sum as an Area/Integral
micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize a given limit-of-sum expression as a Riemann sum and identify the region/integral it represents
definitions: A limit of the form lim_{n->infinity} Sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i) Delta x, where c_i are sample points in a partition of [a,b] with Delta x=(b-a)/n, represents the area under f on [a,b] (a Riemann sum).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a limit of a sum in the form (1/n)*Sum f(i/n)-style, identify the underlying function f and interval [a,b], then state the area it represents.
question_archetypes.example: Recognize lim_{n->infinity} Sum_{i=1}^n (n-i)/n^2 as a Riemann sum, and identify the area it represents.
question_archetypes.answer: Rewrite as Sum (1-i/n)(1/n); this is a Riemann sum for y=1-x on [0,1], a triangle of area 1/2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The 1/n factor signals Delta x=1/n (a partition of [0,1] into n equal pieces), and the remaining factor, once i/n is substituted as x, reveals the function f(x) being sampled.
method_plan: Identify the factor playing the role of Delta x (often 1/n or similar)
Rewrite the remaining factor as f(i/n) or f(a+i*Delta x) to identify f and the interval
State the Riemann sum's limit as the corresponding definite integral
Evaluate geometrically if the region is a simple shape
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of Delta x from the sum's structure
M1: correct identification of f(x) and the interval [a,b]
A1: correct statement of the limit as an integral (or direct geometric area)

common_errors.description: Misidentifying which factor is Delta x versus the sampled function value
Algebra error rewriting the summand in the form needed to spot the pattern

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize a Riemann-sum limit whose sample points correspond to a partition of an interval NOT starting at 0 (e.g. involving 1+i/n), identifying the correct shifted interval.
question_archetypes.example: Express lim_{n->infinity} Sum_{i=1}^n (1/n) sqrt(1+i/n) as a definite integral.
question_archetypes.answer: Integral from 0 to 1 of sqrt(1+x) dx (viewing x=i/n as a partition of [0,1] with f(x)=sqrt(1+x))
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The argument of f contains an added constant (e.g. 1+i/n) — this can be read either as f(x)=sqrt(1+x) on [0,1], or equivalently as a shifted partition of [1,2]; recognizing both interpretations are valid is the key insight.
method_plan: Identify Delta x=1/n and the sample point pattern i/n
Decide whether to absorb the constant shift into f(x) (interval [0,1]) or into the interval bounds (interval [1,2])
State the resulting definite integral in the chosen (simplest) form
Identify the region it represents if requested
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of Delta x and the sample-point pattern
M1: correct handling of the additive shift (either in f or in the limits)
A1: correct final definite integral stated

common_errors.description: Incorrectly shifting both f and the limits simultaneously, effectively double-shifting
Giving an integral that is algebraically equivalent but not simplified to the cleanest recognizable form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize a Riemann-sum limit whose sampled function is trigonometric or otherwise transcendental, including a nontrivial scaling constant multiplying the whole sum.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate lim_{n->infinity} (1/n) Sum_{j=1}^n cos(j*pi/(2n)).
question_archetypes.answer: Recognize as (2/pi) times a Riemann sum for integral_0^(pi/2) cos(x) dx = 1, scaled: limit = 2/pi
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The sum contains an argument like j*pi/(2n) (a partition of [0,pi/2]) but the prefactor (1/n) does not exactly match the needed Delta x=pi/(2n) — a scaling constant must be factored out to correctly match the Riemann-sum pattern before identifying the integral.
method_plan: Identify the true Delta x implied by the argument's step size (e.g. pi/(2n))
Rewrite the given prefactor as (needed Delta x) times a correction constant
Identify the resulting definite integral and evaluate it
Multiply back by the correction constant for the final limit
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the true Delta x from the argument's step size
M1: correct factoring out of the scaling correction constant
A1: correct definite integral identified and evaluated
A1: correct final limit after reapplying the scaling constant

common_errors.description: Failing to correctly factor the scaling constant, leading to a value off by a constant multiple
Assuming the given prefactor is automatically Delta x without checking it matches the argument's actual step size

micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute upper and lower Riemann sums L(f,P) and U(f,P) for a partition, using the actual min/max on each subinterval
definitions: On each [x_{i-1},x_i], let l_i,u_i be points where f attains its min/max. Then L(f,P)=Sum f(l_i)Delta x_i, U(f,P)=Sum f(u_i)Delta x_i, and L(f,P)<=U(f,P) always.
Refining a partition (P1 subset P2) gives L(f,P1)<=L(f,P2)<=U(f,P2)<=U(f,P1).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute L(f,P) and U(f,P) for a monotonic function on a given partition, using the fact that min/max on each subinterval occur at the endpoints.
question_archetypes.example: Compute L(f,P_4) and U(f,P_4) for f(x)=1/x on [1,2] with 4 equal subintervals.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is monotonic (increasing or decreasing) on the interval — this guarantees the min/max on each subinterval occur exactly at its left/right endpoints, so L and U reduce to left-sum/right-sum computations (in the appropriate order).
method_plan: Determine whether f is increasing or decreasing on the interval
Identify which endpoint (left or right) of each subinterval gives the min, and which gives the max
Compute L(f,P) using the min values and U(f,P) using the max values
Verify L(f,P)<=U(f,P)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of monotonic behavior and which endpoint gives min/max
M1: correct computation of L(f,P)
A1: correct computation of U(f,P)
A1: correct verification L<=U

common_errors.description: Confusing upper/lower sums with left/right sums for a DECREASING function (where left endpoint gives the max, not the min)
Arithmetic error evaluating f at the partition points

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute L(f,P) and U(f,P) for a function that is NOT monotonic on the whole interval, requiring the actual min/max to be found on each subinterval individually (possibly at an interior critical point).
question_archetypes.example: Compute L(f,P_2) and U(f,P_2) for f(x)=x^2 on [-1,1] with 2 equal subintervals.
question_archetypes.answer: On [-1,0]: min f=0 at x=0 (interior to that subinterval's boundary), max f=1 at x=-1; on [0,1]: min f=0 at x=0, max f=1 at x=1. L(f,P)=(1)(0+0)=0, U(f,P)=(1)(1+1)=2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function changes from decreasing to increasing (or vice versa) somewhere inside the interval — the min or max on the subinterval containing that turning point occurs at an INTERIOR point, not necessarily at either endpoint.
method_plan: Identify any critical points of f that lie inside the interval
For each subinterval, determine whether the min/max occurs at an endpoint or at an interior critical point
Compute L(f,P) using the correct min on each subinterval, and U(f,P) using the correct max
State both sums
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of any interior critical points affecting min/max
M1: correct L(f,P) using the true minimum on each subinterval
A1: correct U(f,P) using the true maximum on each subinterval

common_errors.description: Assuming min/max always occur at subinterval endpoints, missing an interior critical point
Evaluation error at the interior critical point

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a partition P1 and a refinement P2 (P1 subset P2), verify or use the inequality L(f,P1)<=L(f,P2)<=U(f,P2)<=U(f,P1).
question_archetypes.example: For f(x)=x^2 on [0,2], show L(f,P_2)<=L(f,P_4)<=U(f,P_4)<=U(f,P_2) by computing all four sums.
question_archetypes.answer: Direct computation confirms the chain of inequalities; refining the partition tightens the bracket around the true integral value
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly involves comparing sums from two DIFFERENT partitions where one refines the other — the general theorem about refinement (not the ordinary L<=U for a single partition) is being tested.
method_plan: Compute L and U for the coarser partition P1
Compute L and U for the finer partition P2
Verify the full chain of inequalities L(P1)<=L(P2)<=U(P2)<=U(P1)
Interpret this as the finer partition giving a tighter bracket on the true integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct L and U computed for both partitions
M1: correct verification of the full inequality chain
A1: correct interpretation relating to convergence toward the true integral value

common_errors.description: Assuming refining a partition always changes L and U by a large amount, rather than understanding the bracket only tightens
Computational error in one of the four sums

micro_skills.subtopic: General (Tagged) Riemann Sums and the Definite Integral
micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize a general tagged Riemann sum R(f,P,c) and its limit as the definite integral
definitions: For any tag c_i in [x_{i-1},x_i], R(f,P,c)=Sum f(c_i) Delta x_i satisfies L(f,P)<=R(f,P,c)<=U(f,P), and for integrable f, lim (n(P)->infinity, ||P||->0) R(f,P,c) = integral_a^b f(x) dx.

theorems.name: Theorem 2
theorems.statement: If f is continuous on [a,b], then f is integrable on [a,b].

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a general Riemann sum with a specified tag (e.g. midpoint, or an offset like (2i-1)/n), express its limit as a definite integral.
question_archetypes.example: Express lim_{n->infinity} Sum_{i=1}^n (2/n)(1+(2i-1)/n)^(1/3) as a definite integral.
question_archetypes.answer: Integral_0^2 (1+x)^(1/3) dx (tags c_i=(2i-1)/n lie in [(2i-2)/n,2i/n], an equal partition of [0,2] with Delta x=2/n)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The tag is not a simple endpoint (e.g. (2i-1)/n, a midpoint-style tag) — must verify it lies within the correct subinterval of an equal partition before identifying f and the interval.
method_plan: Identify Delta x from the prefactor
Determine the interval [a,b] and verify the tag c_i lies within the correct subinterval
Identify f(x) from the remaining factor
State the limit as the definite integral integral_a^b f(x) dx
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of Delta x and interval [a,b]
M1: correct verification that the tag lies in the appropriate subinterval
A1: correct final definite integral stated

common_errors.description: Assuming any tag works the same as an endpoint tag without checking it truly lies in [x_{i-1},x_i]
Error identifying the interval [a,b] from the tag's range

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Justify that a given limit of Riemann sums actually converges to a well-defined definite integral by verifying the integrand is continuous (Theorem 2), rather than assuming integrability.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why lim_{n->infinity} Sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i) Delta x_i for f(x)=sqrt(x) on [0,4] is guaranteed to converge to a single value regardless of the choice of tags c_i.
question_archetypes.answer: f(x)=sqrt(x) is continuous on [0,4], so by Theorem 2 it is integrable there; this guarantees L(f,P) and U(f,P) converge to the same value as ||P||->0, so ANY choice of tags c_i gives the same limit, namely integral_0^4 sqrt(x) dx
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks WHY the limit is guaranteed to exist/be tag-independent — a conceptual archetype requiring explicit reference to continuity implying integrability (Theorem 2), not just computing the limit.
method_plan: Verify f is continuous on the interval in question
Invoke Theorem 2 to conclude f is integrable
Explain that integrability means L(f,P) and U(f,P) converge to the same value, forcing any tagged sum to converge there too
State the resulting definite integral
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct verification of continuity
M1: correct invocation of Theorem 2
A1: correct explanation of why tag-independence follows from integrability

common_errors.description: Assuming every bounded function is automatically integrable, without checking continuity (or piecewise continuity)
Computing the integral's value without addressing the actual question of WHY the limit is guaranteed to exist

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain why, for a monotonic function, the left-endpoint Riemann sum always underestimates (or overestimates) the true integral, and the right-endpoint sum does the opposite.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why, if f is continuous and increasing on [a,b], the left-endpoint Riemann sum always underestimates integral_a^b f(x)dx and the right-endpoint sum always overestimates it. What changes if f is decreasing?
question_archetypes.answer: For increasing f, the left endpoint gives the minimum on each subinterval (so the left sum equals L(f,P)<=integral) and the right endpoint gives the maximum (right sum equals U(f,P)>=integral); for decreasing f the roles reverse (left sum becomes U(f,P), right sum becomes L(f,P))
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question is explicitly conceptual, asking to EXPLAIN the systematic bias of left/right sums relative to monotonicity — connects the general L<=integral<=U inequality (Section 5.3) to the specific left/right endpoint sums.
method_plan: State that for increasing f, left endpoint = min on each subinterval, right endpoint = max
Connect this to the definitions of L(f,P) and U(f,P)
Use L(f,P)<=integral<=U(f,P) to conclude the left sum underestimates and right sum overestimates
Explain the reversal for decreasing f
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct identification of left/right endpoint as min/max for increasing f
M1: correct connection to L(f,P)<=integral<=U(f,P)
A1: correct explanation of the reversal for decreasing f

common_errors.description: Stating the bias direction without connecting it to the L(f,P)/U(f,P) inequality as justification
Only addressing the increasing case, omitting the requested explanation for decreasing f

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply linearity, sign-reversal, additivity, and the comparison properties of the definite integral

theorems.name: Theorem 3 (a)-(f)
theorems.statement: (a) integral_a^a f=0. (b) integral_b^a f = -integral_a^b f. (c) integral_a^b (Af+Bg) = A integral_a^b f + B integral_a^b g. (d) integral_a^b f + integral_b^c f = integral_a^c f. (e) f<=g on [a,b] => integral_a^b f <= integral_a^b g. (f) |integral_a^b f| <= integral_a^b |f| (a<=b).
conditions: f,g integrable on an interval containing a,b,c (as relevant to each part)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given values of two separate definite integrals of f and g, use linearity (part c) to evaluate a definite integral of a linear combination of f and g.
question_archetypes.example: Given integral_0^3 f(x)dx=5 and integral_0^3 g(x)dx=-2, evaluate integral_0^3 (4f(x)-3g(x))dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is explicitly a linear combination of two functions whose individual integrals are already given — direct application of linearity (Theorem 3c), no need to find antiderivatives.
method_plan: Split the integral via linearity into separate constant multiples of each given integral
Substitute the given values
Combine to the final numeric answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct application of linearity to split the integral
A1: correct substitution of given values
A1: correct final numeric answer

common_errors.description: Sign error substituting a negative given value
Attempting to find explicit antiderivatives for f,g when linearity alone suffices

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given integrals of f over two adjacent (or overlapping, requiring the reversal property) intervals, use additivity (part d) and sign-reversal (part b) to find the integral over a third related interval.
question_archetypes.example: Given integral_1^5 f(x)dx=8 and integral_3^5 f(x)dx=3, find integral_1^3 f(x)dx.
question_archetypes.answer: integral_1^3 f = integral_1^5 f - integral_3^5 f = 8-3 = 5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three related bounds (1,3,5) are given with two integrals known and a third asked for — additivity integral_a^b+integral_b^c=integral_a^c can be rearranged (using sign-reversal if needed) to solve for the unknown piece.
method_plan: Write the additivity relation linking all three integrals over the given bounds
Rearrange algebraically to isolate the desired unknown integral
Apply the sign-reversal property if the direction of any interval needs flipping
Substitute given values and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct additivity relation set up linking all three integrals
M1: correct algebraic isolation of the unknown integral
A1: correct final numeric value

common_errors.description: Adding the two given integrals directly instead of subtracting, missing that the desired piece is a DIFFERENCE
Sign error applying the reversal property b

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the comparison property (part e) or the absolute-value bound (part f) to establish an inequality about a definite integral without evaluating it exactly.
question_archetypes.example: Without evaluating, show that integral_0^1 sqrt(1+x^4) dx >= 1.
question_archetypes.answer: Since 1+x^4>=1 for all x, sqrt(1+x^4)>=1 on [0,1]; by the comparison property, integral_0^1 sqrt(1+x^4)dx >= integral_0^1 1 dx = 1
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to establish a BOUND or inequality on an integral (often one with no elementary antiderivative) rather than to evaluate it exactly — signals using property (e) or (f) with a simpler comparison function.
method_plan: Find a simpler function that bounds the integrand from above or below on the interval
Apply the comparison property (e) to compare the two integrals
Evaluate the simpler integral exactly
State the resulting inequality for the original integral
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct simpler bounding function identified and justified
M1: correct application of the comparison property
A1: correct final inequality with the simpler integral evaluated

common_errors.description: Choosing a bounding function that does not actually satisfy the required inequality on the whole interval
Not justifying why the chosen bounding function actually bounds the integrand pointwise on the whole interval

micro_skills.micro_skill: Use odd/even symmetry to simplify or evaluate a definite integral over a symmetric interval

theorems.name: Theorem 3 (g)-(h)
theorems.statement: (g) f odd => integral_{-a}^a f dx = 0. (h) f even => integral_{-a}^a f dx = 2*integral_0^a f dx.
conditions: the interval of integration must be symmetric about 0, i.e. [-a,a]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral over a symmetric interval where the integrand is a sum of an odd part and an even (or constant) part, using symmetry to eliminate the odd part.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_{-2}^2 (2+5x) dx using symmetry.
question_archetypes.answer: integral_{-2}^2 2 dx = 8 (rectangle); integral_{-2}^2 5x dx = 0 (odd, symmetric interval); total = 8
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The interval is symmetric about 0 ([-a,a]) and the integrand splits naturally into odd and even/constant pieces — the odd piece can be discarded immediately without further computation.
method_plan: Split the integrand via linearity into its odd and even/constant components
Set the integral of the odd component to 0 by symmetry
Evaluate the even/constant component directly (often geometrically)
Sum for the final answer
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of odd vs. even/constant components
A1: correctly sets the odd component's integral to 0
A1: correct evaluation of the remaining component

common_errors.description: Using the symmetry shortcut (g) or (h) on an interval that is NOT actually symmetric about 0
Misidentifying a term as odd or even (e.g. treating x^2 as odd)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Use the even-function property to reduce a symmetric-interval integral to twice the integral over half the interval, useful when the region has a simpler geometric interpretation on [0,a].
question_archetypes.example: Find the average value of f(x)=sqrt(9-x^2) on [-3,3] by recognizing integral_{-3}^3 sqrt(9-x^2)dx as a semicircle area.
question_archetypes.answer: f is even; integral_{-3}^3 sqrt(9-x^2)dx = semicircle area = (1/2)pi(3)^2 = 9pi/2; average value = (1/6)(9pi/2)=3pi/4
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is even (depends only on x^2, or is otherwise symmetric) and the interval is symmetric about 0 — recognizing the region as a simple geometric shape (semicircle, etc.) over half the interval avoids antiderivative work entirely.
method_plan: Verify f is even
Recognize integral_0^a f(x)dx as a simple geometric area if possible
Apply property (h) to double it for the full symmetric interval
Use the result in whatever further computation is requested (e.g. average value)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct verification of even symmetry
M1: correct geometric identification of the half-interval area
A1: correct doubling and final numeric result

common_errors.description: Forgetting to double the half-interval area when applying property (h)
Arithmetic error identifying the semicircle's radius or area formula

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that the odd/even symmetry shortcuts do NOT apply when the interval is not symmetric about 0, even if the integrand itself is odd or even.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why integral_0^2 x^3 dx cannot be evaluated as 0 using the odd-function symmetry property, even though x^3 is odd.
question_archetypes.answer: The odd-function shortcut integral_{-a}^a f=0 requires the interval to be symmetric about 0; [0,2] is not symmetric about 0, so the shortcut does not apply — the integral must be evaluated directly via the antiderivative, giving integral_0^2 x^3dx = 4, not 0
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand IS odd (or even), which might tempt a student to apply the symmetry shortcut, but the interval of integration is not of the form [-a,a] — a conceptual trap testing whether the interval condition is checked.
method_plan: Check whether the integrand is odd or even
Separately check whether the interval is symmetric about 0
If the interval is NOT symmetric, explicitly state the shortcut does not apply
Evaluate the integral by standard antiderivative methods instead
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct identification that the integrand is odd/even
M1: correct recognition that the interval is not symmetric about 0, so the shortcut fails
A1: correct direct evaluation of the integral instead

common_errors.description: Applying the odd/even symmetry shortcut based solely on the integrand's parity, ignoring the interval's symmetry requirement

micro_skills.subtopic: Mean-Value Theorem for Integrals and Average Value
micro_skills.micro_skill: Compute the average value of a function and find a point guaranteed by the Mean-Value Theorem for Integrals
definitions: Average value: f-bar = (1/(b-a)) integral_a^b f(x) dx.

theorems.name: Theorem 4 (Mean-Value Theorem for Integrals)
theorems.statement: If f is continuous on [a,b], there exists c in [a,b] such that integral_a^b f(x)dx = (b-a) f(c).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Compute the average value of a given function on an interval using an already-known (or easily found) antiderivative.
question_archetypes.example: Find the average value of f(x)=2x on [1,5].
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks specifically for 'average value', which is the direct formula (1/(b-a)) times the definite integral — a routine computation once the antiderivative is known.
method_plan: Find an antiderivative of f
Evaluate the definite integral over [a,b]
Divide by (b-a) to get the average value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct antiderivative and definite integral evaluated
A1: correct division by (b-a)
A1: correct final average value

common_errors.description: Forgetting to divide by (b-a), reporting the plain integral value as the average
Arithmetic error evaluating the antiderivative at the bounds

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find an explicit value c guaranteed by the Mean-Value Theorem for Integrals such that f(c) equals the average value.
question_archetypes.example: Find c in [0,2] guaranteed by the Mean-Value Theorem for Integrals for f(x)=x^2.
question_archetypes.answer: Average value = (1/2)integral_0^2 x^2 dx = 4/3; solve f(c)=c^2=4/3 => c=2/sqrt3 (taking the value in [0,2])
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to find the SPECIFIC point c (not just the average value) — requires computing the average value first, then solving f(c)=average for c within the interval.
method_plan: Compute the average value f-bar via the integral formula
Set f(c) = f-bar and solve for c
Select the solution(s) that lie within [a,b], discarding any outside
State the value(s) of c
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct average value computed
M1: correct equation f(c)=f-bar set up and solved
A1: correct value(s) of c selected within [a,b]

common_errors.description: Reporting the average value itself as 'c', instead of solving f(c)=average for the input c
Failing to discard a solution to f(c)=average that falls outside [a,b]

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Interpret and compute the average value of a physically meaningful rate function (e.g. velocity, temperature) over a time or space interval.
question_archetypes.example: A particle's velocity is v(t)=6t-t^2 for 0<=t<=6. Find its average velocity over this interval.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The average value is requested in a physical/contextual setting (velocity, temperature, etc.) rather than an abstract function — the mathematical procedure is identical, but the answer must be interpreted and stated in context with units.
method_plan: Identify the function and interval from the physical context
Find the antiderivative and evaluate the definite integral
Divide by the interval length
State the average value in context with correct units
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct antiderivative and definite integral evaluated
A1: correct division by interval length
A1: correct final value stated in context with units

common_errors.description: Omitting units or physical interpretation in the final stated answer
Sign or arithmetic error evaluating the antiderivative at the bounds

micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate a definite integral of a piecewise-defined function by splitting at every point of discontinuity
definitions: f is piecewise continuous on [c0,cn] if there are points c0<c1<...<cn and continuous functions F_i on each [c_{i-1},c_i] agreeing with f on the open subinterval; then integral_{c0}^{cn} f dx = Sum_i integral_{c_{i-1}}^{c_i} F_i dx.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral of a function defined by three (or more) different formulas on adjacent subintervals, splitting the integral at every breakpoint.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_0^3 f(x)dx for f(x)=sqrt(1-x^2) on [0,1], f(x)=2 on (1,2], f(x)=x-2 on (2,3].
question_archetypes.answer: pi/4 (quarter circle) + 2 (rectangle) + 1/2 (triangle) = pi/4 + 5/2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is explicitly defined piecewise with different formulas on different subintervals — the integral MUST be split at every breakpoint, evaluating each piece with its own antiderivative or geometric interpretation.
method_plan: Identify every breakpoint where the formula for f changes
Split the integral into one piece per subinterval, using additivity
Evaluate each piece with the correct formula (via antiderivative or geometric area)
Sum all pieces for the total
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of all breakpoints and splitting of the integral
M1: correct evaluation of each individual piece
A1: correct final sum

common_errors.description: Attempting to find one single antiderivative across the entire interval, ignoring the formula changes at breakpoints
Error evaluating one of the individual geometric/antiderivative pieces

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain/demonstrate why a jump discontinuity at a single point (with the function possibly undefined or redefined there) does not affect the value of the definite integral.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why redefining f(2)=100 (a single point) for the piecewise function in the previous example would not change the value of integral_0^3 f(x)dx.
question_archetypes.answer: A single point has zero width (Delta x contribution vanishes in the limit of Riemann sums), so changing the function's value at one isolated point does not affect the integral, even though it does affect whether f is 'continuous' there in the classical sense
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks specifically why a single-point redefinition doesn't matter — a conceptual archetype connecting back to the Riemann-sum definition (isolated points contribute zero measure/width).
method_plan: Recall the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums over subintervals with positive width
Explain that a single point has no width, so it cannot affect any Riemann sum's value in the limit
Conclude the integral's value is unaffected by redefining f at finitely many isolated points
Contrast with an actual interval where f differs (which WOULD change the integral)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct connection to the Riemann-sum/width argument
A1: correct conclusion that isolated point redefinitions don't affect the integral
A1: correct contrast with a genuine subinterval difference, which would matter

common_errors.description: Assuming any discontinuity, no matter how small in extent, changes the value of the integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a piecewise-continuous integral where the pieces have different signs, requiring careful bookkeeping between signed area (plain integral) and total distance/area (which would need absolute values).
question_archetypes.example: A particle's velocity is v(t) defined piecewise, positive on part of [0,8] and negative on the rest. Evaluate integral_0^8 v(t)dt (net displacement) as a piecewise sum, being careful with signs.
question_archetypes.answer: Split at the sign-change point, evaluate each piece with its own sign (not absolute value, since displacement, not distance, is requested), and sum algebraically
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for net displacement (the plain signed integral), not total distance — pieces with negative velocity contribute NEGATIVELY to the sum, unlike a total-distance calculation which would use |v(t)|.
method_plan: Split the integral at the point(s) where the piecewise formula changes (and/or sign changes)
Evaluate each piece using its actual signed value (no absolute value)
Sum all pieces algebraically, preserving signs
State whether the result represents net displacement or another signed quantity as appropriate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct splitting at breakpoints
M1: correct signed evaluation of each piece (no absolute value)
A1: correct final signed sum with correct interpretation stated

common_errors.description: Taking absolute values of each piece when net (signed) displacement, not total distance, was requested
Sign error summing pieces with different signs

micro_skills.subtopic: FTC Part I: Differentiating an Integral with Variable Upper Limit
micro_skills.micro_skill: Differentiate F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt (and generalizations with a function of x as the limit) using FTC Part I and the Chain Rule

theorems.name: Theorem 5 Part I (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus)
theorems.statement: If f is continuous on an interval I containing a, and F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt, then F is differentiable on I and F'(x)=f(x).
conditions: f continuous on I containing a

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt directly using FTC Part I, where the upper limit is exactly x.
question_archetypes.example: Find F'(x) for F(x)=integral_2^x sin(t^3)dt.
question_archetypes.answer: F'(x)=sin(x^3)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The upper limit of integration is exactly x (not a function of x) — a direct, single-step application of FTC Part I with no chain rule needed.
method_plan: Confirm the upper limit is exactly x
Apply FTC Part I: F'(x)=f(x)
Substitute the integrand's formula with t replaced by x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct recognition that FTC Part I applies directly
A1: correct final F'(x)

common_errors.description: Attempting to evaluate the integral first before differentiating, instead of applying the theorem directly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate integral_a^{g(x)} f(t)dt where the upper limit is a function of x (not x itself), requiring the Chain Rule factor g'(x).
question_archetypes.example: Find F'(x) for F(x)=integral_{-4}^{5x} e^{t^2}dt.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The upper limit is a function of x (e.g. 5x, x^2) rather than plain x — the generalized Leibniz formula requires multiplying by the derivative of that upper limit (chain rule).
method_plan: Identify the upper-limit function g(x)
Apply d/dx integral_a^{g(x)} f(t)dt = f(g(x)) g'(x)
Substitute g(x) into f and multiply by g'(x)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of the chain-rule structure
M1: correct substitution of g(x) into f
A1: correct final answer including the g'(x) factor

common_errors.description: Dropping the chain-rule factor g'(x) when the upper limit is a function of x, not just x itself
Substitution error evaluating f at g(x)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate an integral where the VARIABLE is in the lower limit (and the upper limit is constant or another function), requiring the sign-reversal property before applying FTC Part I.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate d/dx integral_{x^2}^5 sin(t^3)dt.
question_archetypes.answer: -2x sin(x^6)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The variable (or a function of the variable) is in the LOWER limit — must flip the integral using integral_a^b=-integral_b^a before FTC Part I (with the chain rule) can be applied cleanly.
method_plan: Rewrite the integral with the variable expression as the upper limit by flipping the sign: integral_{h(x)}^{c} f = -integral_c^{h(x)} f
Apply FTC Part I with the chain rule to the flipped integral
Include the overall negative sign in the final derivative
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct sign-flip to move the variable expression to the upper limit
M1: correct chain-rule application to the flipped integral
A1: correct final answer including the overall negative sign

common_errors.description: Forgetting to flip the sign when the variable is in the lower limit, giving an answer with the wrong overall sign
Chain rule error differentiating the lower-limit function itself (e.g. x^2)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Differentiate an integral where BOTH limits are functions of x, using the full generalized Leibniz formula.
question_archetypes.example: Find d/dx integral_{x}^{x^2} sqrt(1+t^2) dt.
question_archetypes.answer: 2x*sqrt(1+x^4) - sqrt(1+x^2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both the upper and lower limits are (different) functions of x — requires the two-term generalized Leibniz formula, combining a chain-rule term for each limit with the correct signs.
method_plan: Identify g(x)=upper limit, h(x)=lower limit
Apply d/dx integral_{h(x)}^{g(x)} f(t)dt = f(g(x))g'(x) - f(h(x))h'(x)
Compute g'(x), h'(x), and substitute into the formula
Simplify the resulting expression
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of g(x) and h(x)
M1: correct application of the two-term Leibniz formula with correct signs
A1: correct final simplified derivative

common_errors.description: Forgetting the minus sign on the lower-limit term
Chain rule error differentiating one of the two limit functions

micro_skills.subtopic: FTC Part II: Evaluating Definite Integrals via Antiderivatives
micro_skills.micro_skill: Evaluate a definite integral using any antiderivative via FTC Part II
definitions: F(x)|_a^b = F(b)-F(a); the constant of integration cancels in this evaluation, so it is omitted for definite integrals.

theorems.name: Theorem 5 Part II (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus)
theorems.statement: If G is ANY antiderivative of f on I (G'=f), then for any b in I, integral_a^b f(x)dx = G(b)-G(a).
conditions: f continuous on an interval I containing a,b
G is any antiderivative of f on I

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral of a polynomial (or simple elementary function) directly via FTC Part II, and interpret it as the area under the curve.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area under y=3x-x^2 above the x-axis, between its roots.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for an area under a curve above the x-axis between two roots — first find the roots (bounds), then apply FTC Part II directly with a straightforward antiderivative.
method_plan: Find the bounds of integration (e.g. the roots, if the region is 'under the curve')
Find an antiderivative of the integrand
Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper and lower bounds and subtract
State the final area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct bounds identified
M1: correct antiderivative found
A1: correct evaluation and subtraction giving the final area

common_errors.description: Arithmetic error evaluating the antiderivative at the bounds
Including a +C in the definite-integral evaluation, which is unnecessary and can lead to errors if handled inconsistently

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Solve an integral equation where an unknown function f is defined implicitly in terms of its own integral, by differentiating both sides (FTC Part I) to obtain a differential equation, then using the original equation to pin down the constant.
question_archetypes.example: Solve the integral equation f(x) = 2 + 3*integral_4^x f(t)dt.
question_archetypes.answer: Differentiating: f'(x)=3f(x), so f(x)=Ce^{3x}; substituting x=4 into the original equation gives f(4)=2, so C=2e^{-12}, giving f(x)=2e^{3x-12}
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The unknown function f appears both outside AND inside its own integral in the given equation — differentiate both sides using FTC Part I to convert to a differential equation, then use the ORIGINAL equation (not the differentiated one) at the integral's lower limit to find the constant.
method_plan: Differentiate both sides of the integral equation using FTC Part I
Solve the resulting differential equation (often separable, giving an exponential form)
Substitute x = (the integral's lower limit) into the ORIGINAL equation to find the initial value f(lower limit)
Use this initial condition to solve for the constant of integration
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct differentiation of both sides via FTC Part I
M1: correct general solution of the resulting differential equation
A1: correct use of the original equation at the lower limit to find the initial condition
A1: correct final explicit formula for f(x)

common_errors.description: Trying to find the initial condition from the DIFFERENTIATED equation rather than plugging the lower limit into the ORIGINAL integral equation
Solving the differential equation incorrectly (e.g. missing the exponential form for f'=kf)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that FTC Part II cannot be applied directly to an integral whose integrand is discontinuous (in particular unbounded) somewhere in the interval, and explain the correct (improper-integral) treatment instead.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why integral_{-1}^1 dx/x is NOT equal to ln|x| evaluated from -1 to 1 (which naively gives 0).
question_archetypes.answer: 1/x is discontinuous (unbounded) at x=0, which lies INSIDE [-1,1], so FTC Part II's hypothesis (continuity on the whole interval) fails; the integral is not even integrable in the ordinary sense there — it must be treated as an improper integral, split at the singularity, and in fact diverges
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question presents a plausible-looking but WRONG application of FTC (naive antiderivative evaluation) to an integrand with a hidden interior discontinuity — a conceptual/diagnostic archetype testing the continuity hypothesis of Theorem 5.
method_plan: Identify any point in the interval where the integrand is discontinuous or unbounded
State that FTC Part II requires continuity of f on the whole interval, which fails here
Explain that naive antiderivative evaluation is invalid and gives a meaningless/wrong result
State the correct approach (splitting as an improper integral) without necessarily fully evaluating it
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct identification of the interior discontinuity
M1: correct explanation that this violates FTC Part II's continuity hypothesis
A1: correct statement of the proper (improper-integral) treatment required instead

common_errors.description: Trusting the naive antiderivative-evaluation result without checking the continuity hypothesis first

micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize and apply u=g(x) substitution to reduce an indefinite integral to a memorized elementary form
definitions: If u=g(x), du=g'(x)dx, then integral f'(g(x)) g'(x) dx = integral f'(u) du = f(g(x))+C.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate an expression where the derivative of a natural inner function appears (up to a constant) as a factor, using u-substitution.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral x/(x^2+1) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand contains an inner expression (e.g. x^2+1) whose derivative (2x, up to a constant) is present as a multiplicative factor — a direct cue for u=inner expression.
method_plan: Let u = the inner expression
Compute du and match it (up to a constant) to the remaining factor in the integrand
Rewrite the integral entirely in terms of u and integrate
Substitute back u=g(x) and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct choice of u and computation of du
M1: correct rewriting of the integral purely in terms of u
A1: correct antiderivative in u, substituted back to x with +C

common_errors.description: Substituting u but leaving a leftover x term that doesn't cancel, not noticing du doesn't fully match
Forgetting +C on the indefinite integral

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a rational expression with an irreducible quadratic denominator by first completing the square, then substituting to match the arctan or arcsin elementary form.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral dx/(x^2+4x+5).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The denominator is an irreducible quadratic NOT already in the form x^2+a^2 or a^2-x^2 — completing the square first is required before the substitution t=(x-h) reveals the standard arctan/arcsin form.
method_plan: Complete the square in the quadratic denominator
Substitute t = x - h (the shift from completing the square)
Match to the standard arctan (or arcsin) elementary form
Convert back to x and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct completing of the square
M1: correct substitution and matching to the standard form
A1: correct final answer in terms of x with +C

common_errors.description: Error completing the square (wrong shift or constant)
Attempting a substitution before completing the square, when the quadratic isn't yet in x^2+a^2 form

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given an integral that superficially resembles a substitution candidate but the needed derivative factor is actually absent, recognize substitution does not apply cleanly and identify what IS needed instead.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why integral sqrt(x^2+1) dx (without an extra x factor) cannot be solved by the substitution u=x^2+1.
question_archetypes.answer: du=2x dx requires an x factor in the integrand, which is absent here; a trig or hyperbolic substitution (Section 6.3) is needed instead, not ordinary u-substitution
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand LOOKS similar to a standard substitution pattern (inner function present) but the necessary derivative factor g'(x) is simply not present as a multiplier — a conceptual trap distinguishing 'looks similar' from 'substitution actually works'.
method_plan: Attempt the natural substitution u=inner expression and compute du
Check whether du (or a constant multiple) is actually present in the integrand
If not, conclude ordinary substitution fails and identify the correct alternative technique needed
State the alternative technique by name if known
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct attempted substitution and computation of du
M1: correct recognition that the needed factor is absent
A1: correct identification of what technique is actually needed instead

common_errors.description: Forcing the substitution anyway and introducing an incorrect extra factor to make it 'work'
Giving up without identifying what technique would actually apply

micro_skills.micro_skill: Apply u-substitution to a definite integral, correctly handling the limits of integration (Method I or Method II, not mixed)

theorems.name: Theorem 6 (Substitution in a definite integral)
theorems.statement: If g(a)=A, g(b)=B, and f is continuous on the range of g, then integral_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)dx = integral_A^B f(u)du.
conditions: f continuous on the range of g

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral by substitution, converting the limits of integration to u-values (Method I) and never converting back to x.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate I=integral_0^8 cos(sqrt(x+1))/sqrt(x+1) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: u=sqrt(x+1), limits x=0=>u=1, x=8=>u=3: I=2*integral_1^3 cos(u)du = 2sin(3)-2sin(1)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The substitution is clean and the problem is a definite integral — Method I (converting the limits to u-values immediately) avoids ever needing to substitute back to x, which is usually the more efficient approach.
method_plan: Choose u=g(x) and compute du
Convert both limits of integration from x-values to u-values using u=g(x)
Rewrite the entire integral (integrand AND limits) in terms of u
Evaluate the u-integral directly using the NEW limits, without converting back to x
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct u and du
M1: correct converted limits
A1: correct u-integral evaluated using the new limits

common_errors.description: Converting the limits to u-values but then mistakenly substituting the ORIGINAL x-limits back in at the end
Error evaluating g at one of the endpoints to find the new limit

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral by substitution using Method II: keep the original x-limits, find the antiderivative in terms of u, convert it back to x, then evaluate at the original x-limits.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_0^{pi/4} tan(x) sec^2(x) dx by finding the antiderivative in terms of u=tan(x), converting back to x, and evaluating at the original limits.
question_archetypes.answer: Antiderivative in u: u^2/2; convert back: tan^2(x)/2; evaluate at pi/4 and 0: (1/2)(1)-(1/2)(0)=1/2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to keep the ORIGINAL x-limits (Method II) rather than converting them — requires converting the found antiderivative back to a function of x before plugging in the original bounds.
method_plan: Choose u=g(x), find the antiderivative in terms of u (without changing the limits)
Convert the antiderivative back to a function of x by substituting u=g(x) again
Evaluate this x-antiderivative at the ORIGINAL x-limits
State the final value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct u and antiderivative found in terms of u
M1: correct conversion of the antiderivative back to x
A1: correct evaluation at the original x-limits

common_errors.description: Mixing the two methods: converting the limits to u-values AND also converting the antiderivative back to x, effectively doing the limit-substitution twice
Error converting the antiderivative back to x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize a subtle case where the substitution's validity requires checking that f is continuous on the ENTIRE range of g(x) over [a,b], not just at the endpoints, catching a case where this fails.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why substituting u=x^2 in integral_{-1}^{2} x*csc(x^2) dx is problematic if csc is evaluated at u=0 somewhere within the range of g.
question_archetypes.answer: g(x)=x^2 takes the value 0 at x=0, which lies in [-1,2]; since csc(u) is undefined (discontinuous) at u=0, the hypothesis 'f continuous on the range of g' fails, so Theorem 6 cannot be applied naively — the original integral may not even be proper/convergent
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The substitution function g(x) passes through a value where f is undefined or discontinuous SOMEWHERE within the interval [a,b] (not just possibly at an endpoint) — a conceptual trap testing the full hypothesis of Theorem 6, not just the endpoint computation.
method_plan: Determine the range of g(x) over the full interval [a,b], not just at the endpoints
Check whether f is continuous over that ENTIRE range
If f has a discontinuity within that range, conclude Theorem 6's hypothesis fails
State the correct implication (the naive substitution result cannot be trusted; the integral may be improper or undefined)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct determination of the full range of g over [a,b]
M1: correct identification of a discontinuity of f within that range
A1: correct conclusion that Theorem 6 does not apply, with explanation

common_errors.description: Only checking continuity of f at the two endpoint values of g, not over its entire range on [a,b]

micro_skills.subtopic: Integrals of tan, cot, sec, csc
micro_skills.micro_skill: Integrate tan, cot, sec, and csc (and simple combinations) using their memorized antiderivatives

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate tan, cot, sec, or csc of a linear argument (ax+b), applying the memorized formula with the appropriate 1/a scaling.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral sec(3x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: (1/3)ln|sec(3x)+tan(3x)|+C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The argument of the trig function is linear (ax rather than just x) — apply the memorized formula and divide by the coefficient a (reverse chain rule), analogous to the e^(kx) pattern.
method_plan: Identify the argument as ax+b and the corresponding memorized formula
Apply the formula, scaling by 1/a for the linear argument
Add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct formula selected
A1: correct 1/a scaling applied
A1: +C included

common_errors.description: Forgetting the 1/a scaling factor for the linear argument
Omitting +C

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Derive (rather than just quote) the antiderivative of sec(x) using the classic multiply-by-(sec x+tan x)/(sec x+tan x) trick.
question_archetypes.example: Derive integral sec(x)dx = ln|sec(x)+tan(x)|+C from scratch.
question_archetypes.answer: Multiply sec(x) by (sec x+tan x)/(sec x+tan x): integrand becomes (sec^2 x+sec x tan x)/(sec x+tan x), whose numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so the antiderivative is ln|sec x+tan x|+C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to DERIVE the formula (not just apply it) — tests the classic 'multiply by a clever form of 1' trick that converts the integrand into an f'/f pattern.
method_plan: Multiply sec(x) by (sec x+tan x)/(sec x+tan x)
Simplify the numerator and recognize it equals the derivative of the denominator (sec x+tan x)
Apply the integral f'/f = ln|f| pattern
State the resulting antiderivative with +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct multiplication trick set up
M1: correct recognition of the f'/f pattern
A1: correct final antiderivative with +C

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the numerator after multiplying is exactly the derivative of the denominator
Expansion error multiplying sec(x) by the clever form of 1

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate a sum/difference involving one of tan/cot/sec/csc combined with another elementary or trig-derivative term (e.g. sec^2, csc*cot).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral (sec^2(3x) - 4 csc(2x)cot(2x)) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand combines a term needing a DIRECT derivative-formula lookup (e.g. sec^2 x -> tan x, or csc x cot x -> -csc x) alongside a term needing the ln-based tan/cot/sec/csc antiderivative — each term must be matched to its own distinct rule.
method_plan: Split the integral via linearity into individual terms
Match each term to its correct derivative-based or ln-based antiderivative formula
Apply the correct 1/a scaling for any linear argument in each term
Combine with correct signs and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct antiderivative for the direct-lookup term (e.g. sec^2 -> tan)
M1: correct antiderivative for the ln-based tan/cot/sec/csc term
A1: correctly combined with correct signs and +C

common_errors.description: Confusing the antiderivative of csc(x)cot(x) (which is -csc(x), a direct lookup) with the antiderivative of csc(x) alone (the ln-based formula)
Sign error on the csc/cot term

micro_skills.micro_skill: Integrate integral sin^m(x)cos^n(x)dx when at least one of m,n is odd, by peeling off one factor and substituting
definitions: If the power of cos(x) is odd, peel off one factor of cos(x) and use cos^2(x)=1-sin^2(x), then substitute u=sin(x) (symmetric idea for odd powers of sin(x)).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate sin^m(x)cos^n(x) where n (the cosine power) is odd, peeling off one cosine factor and substituting u=sin(x).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral sin^3(x)cos^8(x) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The exponent on cos(x) is odd (here implicitly via the sin^3 term after rewriting) — actually here sin has the odd power 3; peel off one sin(x) factor and use sin^2=1-cos^2, substituting u=cos(x).
method_plan: Peel off one factor of the odd-power trig function (leaving an even power remaining)
Rewrite the remaining even power using the Pythagorean identity in terms of the OTHER function
Substitute u = the other function (matching the peeled-off factor times dx to du)
Integrate the resulting polynomial in u and substitute back
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct peeling off of one factor and rewriting via the Pythagorean identity
M1: correct substitution u=cos(x) (or sin(x)) with du matching
A1: correct polynomial integration in u
A1: correct final answer in x with +C

common_errors.description: Peeling off a factor from the EVEN-power term instead of the odd-power term, leaving an unmatched du
Binomial expansion error rewriting (1-u^2)^k before integrating termwise

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate a definite integral of sin^m(x)cos^n(x) on a standard interval (e.g. [0,pi/2]) where one power is odd, converting limits to u-values.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral_0^{pi/2} sin^3(x)cos^3(x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: 1/12 (peel off cos(x): rewrite as sin^3(x)(1-sin^2(x))cos(x); u=sin(x), limits x=0=>u=0, x=pi/2=>u=1: integral_0^1 u^3(1-u^2)du = [u^4/4-u^6/6]_0^1 = 1/4-1/6 = 1/12)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A definite integral over a standard bound (0 to pi/2, or similar) with one odd power — after substitution, remember to convert the LIMITS to u-values (Method I) to avoid re-converting back to x.
method_plan: Identify which power is odd and peel off the corresponding factor
Substitute u=the other trig function, converting the limits of integration to u-values
Integrate the resulting polynomial in u using the NEW limits
State the final numeric value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct peeling and substitution set up
M1: correct converted limits
A1: correct final numeric value after integrating in u

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert the limits of integration when substituting, then evaluating at the wrong (original x) bounds
Sign error when the substitution reverses the order of the limits

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate sin^m(x)cos^n(x) where BOTH m and n are odd, recognizing that either factor may be peeled off, and choosing the one giving the simpler resulting polynomial.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral sin^3(x)cos^3(x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: Peel off cos(x): integral sin^3(x)(1-sin^2(x))cos(x)dx, u=sin(x): integral u^3(1-u^2)du = u^4/4-u^6/6+C = sin^4(x)/4-sin^6(x)/6+C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Both exponents are odd — either substitution (u=sin x or u=cos x) works equally well by symmetry, so choosing either and proceeding consistently is the key skill (rather than being stuck deciding).
method_plan: Recognize either factor could be peeled off since both powers are odd
Choose one (arbitrarily, or based on which gives a lower resulting polynomial degree) and peel off one factor of it
Rewrite the remaining even power via the Pythagorean identity and substitute
Integrate and convert back to the original variable
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct recognition that either substitution choice is valid
M1: correct peeling and Pythagorean rewriting
A1: correct polynomial integration in u
A1: correct final answer in x with +C

common_errors.description: Attempting both substitutions simultaneously or switching mid-computation, leading to a mixed and incorrect result
Sign or expansion error in the resulting polynomial

micro_skills.subtopic: Even Powers of Sine/Cosine via Double-Angle Formulas
micro_skills.micro_skill: Integrate sin^n(x) or cos^n(x) (or products where BOTH powers are even) using the double-angle half-angle identities
definitions: cos^2(x) = (1/2)(1+cos(2x)), sin^2(x) = (1/2)(1-cos(2x)) — used when peeling off a single factor is not possible (all powers even).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate sin^2(x) or cos^2(x) directly using the memorized half-angle antiderivative formula.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral cos^2(x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: (1/2)(x+sin(x)cos(x))+C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The integrand is exactly sin^2(x) or cos^2(x) to the first power — a direct application of the memorized half-angle antiderivative, without needing to re-derive it from scratch.
method_plan: Recall (or re-derive) cos^2(x)=(1/2)(1+cos(2x)) or sin^2(x)=(1/2)(1-cos(2x))
Integrate termwise
State the antiderivative in the compact memorized form or the expanded (x+sin x cos x) form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct half-angle identity applied
A1: correct termwise integration
A1: correct final form with +C

common_errors.description: Attempting u-substitution directly on sin^2(x) or cos^2(x) with no odd factor to peel off, getting stuck
Sign error in the half-angle identity for sin^2 vs cos^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate sin^4(x) or cos^4(x) by applying the double-angle formula TWICE (squaring the half-angle identity, then reducing the resulting cos^2(2x) term again).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral sin^4(x) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The power is 4 (or higher even power) — a single application of the half-angle formula leaves a squared cosine term (cos^2(2x)) that itself needs a SECOND application of the half-angle identity before it can be integrated.
method_plan: Apply the half-angle identity once to get an expression in cos(2x)
Square the resulting binomial, producing a cos^2(2x) term
Apply the half-angle identity a SECOND time to cos^2(2x), converting it to a cos(4x) term
Integrate the fully expanded expression termwise
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct first application of the half-angle identity and squaring
M1: correct second application of the half-angle identity to the cos^2(2x) term
A1: correct termwise integration of all resulting pieces
A1: correctly simplified final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Stopping after only one application of the half-angle formula, leaving an un-integrated cos^2(2x) term
Expansion error squaring the binomial (1+/-cos(2x))^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate sin^m(x)cos^n(x) where BOTH m and n are even (so no factor can be peeled off), requiring repeated half-angle reduction on the product.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral sin^2(x)cos^2(x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: Using sin^2 x cos^2 x = (1/4)sin^2(2x) = (1/8)(1-cos(4x)): integral = x/8 - sin(4x)/32 + C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: BOTH exponents in the product are even — neither the odd-power peel-off technique nor a single half-angle substitution suffices; recognizing sin(x)cos(x)=(1/2)sin(2x) first often simplifies the product dramatically before any further reduction.
method_plan: Recognize sin(x)cos(x)=(1/2)sin(2x) and rewrite the product to reduce the total degree if helpful
Apply the half-angle identity to any remaining even power
Integrate the fully expanded expression termwise
Simplify the final result
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct use of the double-angle product identity to simplify the integrand
M1: correct subsequent half-angle reduction of any remaining power
A1: correct termwise integration
A1: correct simplified final answer with +C

common_errors.description: Expanding sin^2(x) and cos^2(x) separately via half-angle formulas without first noticing the sin(x)cos(x)=(1/2)sin(2x) shortcut, leading to much messier algebra
Error in the repeated half-angle reduction of sin^2(2x)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Integrate powers of sec(x) and tan(x) (or csc/cot) using sec^2=1+tan^2 and substitution u=tan(x)
definitions: Use sec^2(x)=1+tan^2(x) (or csc^2(x)=1+cot^2(x)) with u=tan(x) (or u=cot(x)), UNLESS the secant power is odd and the tangent power is even (that case needs integration by parts instead).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate tan^m(x)sec^n(x) where n (the secant power) is even, peeling off sec^2(x) and substituting u=tan(x).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral tan^3(x)sec^4(x) dx.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The power of sec(x) is even — peel off sec^2(x) as the 'du' factor (since d/dx tan(x)=sec^2(x)) and rewrite the remaining even power of sec as (1+tan^2(x)) to reduce entirely to a polynomial in u=tan(x).
method_plan: Peel off a factor of sec^2(x) (matching du for u=tan(x))
Rewrite the remaining even power of sec(x) using sec^2=1+tan^2
Substitute u=tan(x) and integrate the resulting polynomial
Convert back to x and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct peeling off of sec^2(x) and substitution u=tan(x)
M1: correct rewriting of the remaining even secant power via 1+tan^2
A1: correct polynomial integration in u
A1: correct final answer in x with +C

common_errors.description: Peeling off the wrong factor (e.g. peeling off tan(x) instead of sec^2(x)), leaving a du mismatch
Binomial expansion error rewriting (1+u^2)^k

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Integrate tan^m(x)sec^n(x) where m (the tangent power) is odd, peeling off sec(x)tan(x) and substituting u=sec(x).
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate integral tan^3(x)sec(x) dx.
question_archetypes.answer: sec^3(x)/3 - sec(x) + C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The power of tan(x) is odd — peel off one factor of sec(x)tan(x) (matching du for u=sec(x), since d/dx sec(x)=sec(x)tan(x)) and rewrite the remaining even power of tan(x) using tan^2=sec^2-1.
method_plan: Peel off a factor of sec(x)tan(x) (matching du for u=sec(x))
Rewrite the remaining even power of tan(x) using tan^2=sec^2-1
Substitute u=sec(x) and integrate the resulting polynomial
Convert back to x and add +C
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct peeling off of sec(x)tan(x) and substitution u=sec(x)
M1: correct rewriting of the remaining even tangent power via sec^2-1
A1: correct polynomial integration in u
A1: correct final answer in x with +C

common_errors.description: Confusing which substitution (u=tan or u=sec) matches which peeled-off factor
Sign error rewriting tan^2 as sec^2-1

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize the exceptional case where the secant power is odd AND the tangent power is even (or sec(x) alone to an odd power), where neither standard substitution works, requiring integration by parts instead.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why integral sec^3(x) dx cannot be solved by the standard tan/sec substitution techniques, and identify the correct approach.
