question_archetypes.answer: Here the tangent power is 0 (even) and the secant power is 3 (odd) — neither peeling off sec^2 (no even leftover matches) nor peeling off sec*tan (no tan factor exists) works; this case requires integration by parts (Section 6.1), giving integral sec^3(x)dx = (1/2)sec(x)tan(x)+(1/2)ln|sec(x)+tan(x)|+C
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The tangent power is even (possibly zero) while the secant power is odd — the diagnostic exception explicitly called out in the substitution rules, signaling the student must switch techniques entirely (to integration by parts) rather than force a substitution.
method_plan: Check the parity of both the tangent and secant powers
Recognize that odd-secant/even-tangent is the exceptional case where standard substitution does not reduce the integral
State that integration by parts is required instead
Quote or derive the known result for integral sec^3(x)dx if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct parity check identifying the exceptional case
M1: correct conclusion that substitution alone fails here
A1: correct identification/statement of the by-parts approach and/or known result

common_errors.description: Attempting to force one of the two standard substitutions anyway, getting stuck with an unmatched integrand
Not recognizing this specific parity combination as the signal to switch techniques

micro_skills.micro_skill: Find the total unsigned area between a curve and the x-axis by splitting at zeros and using absolute value
definitions: Total (unsigned) area between y=f(x) and the x-axis: integral_a^b |f(x)|dx = A1+A2, versus the plain (signed) integral_a^b f(x)dx = A1-A2 when f changes sign.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the total area between a polynomial and the x-axis over an interval where the polynomial changes sign, splitting the integral at each root.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area of the finite region bounded by y=x^3-x and y=0.
question_archetypes.answer: Roots at -1,0,1; total area = integral_{-1}^0(x^3-x)dx + integral_0^1 -(x^3-x)dx = 1/4+1/4 = 1/2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The region is bounded by the curve and the x-axis (y=0) over an interval containing a sign change — must split at every root and take the absolute value (or flip the sign) of each piece before summing.
method_plan: Find all roots of f(x)=0 within the region
Determine the sign of f on each subinterval between consecutive roots
Integrate each piece using the correct sign (or |f|) so every piece contributes positively
Sum all pieces for the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct roots found
M1: correct sign determined on each subinterval
A1: correct integration of each piece with the correct sign
A1: correct final total area (a positive number)

common_errors.description: Computing the plain signed integral over the whole interval, letting positive and negative pieces cancel instead of splitting at the roots
Sign error on the piece where f is negative

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a velocity function that changes sign, compute total distance traveled (requiring |v(t)|) and contrast it with net displacement (the plain integral).
question_archetypes.example: A particle moves so that its velocity is v(t)=6t-t^2 for 0<=t<=8. Explain why integral_0^8 |v(t)|dt, rather than integral_0^8 v(t)dt, gives total distance traveled, and compute it.
question_archetypes.answer: v(t)>0 on (0,6), v(t)<0 on (6,8); total distance = integral_0^6(6t-t^2)dt + integral_6^8(t^2-6t)dt = 36+44/3 = 152/3 m
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The word 'total distance' (as opposed to 'displacement' or 'net change in position') signals that direction-reversals must be accounted for via |v(t)|, splitting the integral at every sign change of v.
method_plan: Find where v(t) changes sign (solve v(t)=0)
Split the interval at these points
Integrate |v(t)| on each piece (using -v where v is negative)
Sum all pieces for the total distance
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of sign-change point(s) of v(t)
M1: correct splitting and sign-correction on each piece
A1: correct evaluation of each piece
A1: correct final total distance, with explanation of why |v| (not v) was needed

common_errors.description: Computing the plain (signed) integral of v(t), which gives net displacement rather than total distance, and letting the two pieces partially cancel
Sign or arithmetic error on the piece where v(t) is negative

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the total area between a curve with MULTIPLE sign changes (three or more roots) and the x-axis over a longer interval.
question_archetypes.example: Find the total area between y=sin(x) and the x-axis on [0,2*pi].
question_archetypes.answer: Roots at 0,pi,2pi; total area = integral_0^pi sin(x)dx + integral_pi^{2pi} -sin(x)dx = 2+2 = 4
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The interval spans multiple full sign changes of the integrand (more than one root strictly inside the interval) — every subinterval between consecutive roots must be handled with its own correct sign before summing.
method_plan: Find ALL roots of f(x)=0 within the given interval
Determine the sign of f on each of the resulting subintervals
Integrate each piece with the correct sign so every contribution is positive
Sum all pieces for the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of ALL roots within the interval
M1: correct sign determined on every subinterval
A1: correct integration of each piece
A1: correct final total (positive) area

common_errors.description: Missing one of the roots inside the interval, merging two subintervals with opposite signs incorrectly
Sign error on one of the several pieces

micro_skills.micro_skill: Find the area between two curves y=f(x) and y=g(x) using vertical strips, integrating (upper-lower)
definitions: Area between y=f(x) (lower) and y=g(x) (upper), a<=x<=b: A = integral_a^b (g(x)-f(x))dx. More generally, if the curves cross, A = integral_a^b |f(x)-g(x)|dx, split at the crossing points.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area of a single region enclosed between two curves that cross exactly twice (at the region's two endpoints), with one curve consistently above the other in between.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area between y=x^2-2x and y=4-x^2.
question_archetypes.answer: Curves meet at x=-1,2; A = integral_{-1}^2 [(4-x^2)-(x^2-2x)]dx = integral_{-1}^2 (4-2x^2+2x)dx = 9
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The two curves intersect at exactly two points bounding a single enclosed region, with a clear 'upper' and 'lower' curve throughout that interval — no need to split further.
method_plan: Solve f(x)=g(x) to find the bounding intersection points
Determine which curve is on top (upper) between those points, e.g. by testing a value
Integrate (upper - lower) from the left intersection to the right intersection
Simplify to the final area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection points found
M1: correct identification of upper vs. lower curve
A1: correct integral set up and evaluated
A1: correct final positive area

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the TOTAL area between two curves that cross more than twice within a given interval, splitting the integral at every crossing point.
question_archetypes.example: Find the total area between y=sin(x) and y=cos(x) on [0,2*pi].
question_archetypes.answer: Curves cross at x=pi/4, 5pi/4; split into three pieces and sum absolute contributions: total area = 4*sqrt(2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The two curves cross more than twice within the given interval (here twice, giving three subintervals of alternating 'winner') — the WHICH curve is on top switches at each crossing, so each piece must be integrated with the correct sign (or via |f-g|) separately.
method_plan: Solve f(x)=g(x) to find ALL crossing points within the interval
Determine which curve is on top on each resulting subinterval
Integrate (upper-lower) on each subinterval separately
Sum all (positive) pieces for the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of ALL crossing points
M1: correct determination of the upper curve on each subinterval
A1: correct integration of each individual piece
A1: correct final total area summed correctly

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area of a region bounded by three (or more) different curves/lines, requiring the region to be split into pieces where a DIFFERENT pair of curves forms the top/bottom boundary.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area of the region bounded by y=x^2, y=8-x^2, and the y-axis (x=0), for x>=0.
question_archetypes.answer: The two parabolas intersect where x^2=8-x^2 => x=2; for 0<=x<=2, the region between them is bounded above by y=8-x^2 and below by y=x^2 (both curves are directly given, no further split needed here since x=0 is already a boundary): A = integral_0^2[(8-x^2)-x^2]dx = integral_0^2(8-2x^2)dx = 16-16/3=32/3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Three or more curves/lines are given as boundaries — first sketch (or reason about) the region to determine over which x-range each pair of curves forms the actual top/bottom boundary, since this may change partway through the region.
method_plan: Determine the region's boundaries by finding all pairwise intersection points among the given curves
Identify which pair of curves (and which is upper/lower) applies on each relevant x-subinterval
Integrate (upper-lower) separately on each subinterval
Sum the pieces for the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection points found among all boundary curves
M1: correct identification of which curves bound the region on each subinterval
A1: correct integration of each piece
A1: correct final total area

definitions: If R lies between x=f(y) (left) and x=g(y) (right) for c<=y<=d, A = integral_c^d (g(y)-f(y))dy.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Recognize that a region is more naturally described as left/right boundaries in terms of y (e.g. a sideways parabola) and set up the area integral in y instead of x.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area of the region right of x=y^2-12 and left of y=x.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: One boundary is naturally expressed as x=f(y) (e.g. x=y^2-12, a sideways parabola) — integrating in x would require solving for y as a multi-branched function, while integrating in y treats each curve as a single-valued function of y directly.
method_plan: Rewrite all boundaries as x=(function of y) if not already in that form
Solve for the y-values where the boundaries intersect
Determine which curve is to the right (larger x) and which is to the left on the relevant y-range
Integrate (right - left) with respect to y over the y-interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rewriting of boundaries as functions of y
M1: correct intersection y-values found
A1: correct identification of right vs. left curve
A1: correct integral set up and evaluated in y

common_errors.description: Attempting to integrate in x for a region that is much more naturally described in y, requiring solving for two separate branches (upper and lower halves) unnecessarily

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area of a region where the left or right boundary (as a function of y) changes partway through the y-range, requiring the integral to be split.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area enclosed by x=y^2 and x=y+2 for the full range of y where they overlap, noting whether a single integral in y suffices or a split is needed.
question_archetypes.answer: Intersections at y^2=y+2 => y=-1,2; on this range x=y+2 is consistently to the right of x=y^2, so a SINGLE integral integral_{-1}^2[(y+2)-y^2]dy = 9/2 suffices here (no split needed, since only two curves bound the whole range)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Before assuming a single integral suffices, check whether the SAME pair of curves bounds left/right throughout the full y-range — if a third curve becomes the boundary partway through, the integral must be split there.
method_plan: Find all relevant y-intersections among the boundary curves
Check whether the same pair of curves remains the left/right boundary throughout, or whether a different curve takes over partway
If a split is needed, integrate each piece separately with the correct left/right curves
Sum the pieces (or use the single integral if no split is actually needed) for the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection y-values found
M1: correct check for whether a split is actually necessary
A1: correct integral(s) set up with correctly identified left/right boundaries
A1: correct final total area

common_errors.description: Assuming a split is always needed (or never needed) without actually checking which curves bound the region throughout the range
Error finding the intersection y-values

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a region describable either way, compare the x-integral and y-integral setups and justify which is more efficient before computing.
question_archetypes.example: For the region bounded by y=sqrt(x), y=0, and x=4, compare setting up the area as an x-integral versus a y-integral, and compute using the simpler one.
question_archetypes.answer: As an x-integral: A=integral_0^4 sqrt(x)dx = 16/3 (single simple integral); as a y-integral it would require A=integral_0^2 (4-y^2)dy, also straightforward here — both work, but the x-integral requires no rewriting of the boundary, making it marginally simpler
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to COMPARE or justify a choice of integration variable before computing — a strategic/diagnostic archetype rather than a purely computational one, testing the judgment of when integrating in y is genuinely preferable.
method_plan: Sketch or describe the region and identify its boundaries in both x-terms and y-terms
Set up the area integral both ways symbolically
Compare which setup avoids solving for multi-valued branches or splitting the integral
Compute using the more efficient setup
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct symbolic setup of both the x-integral and y-integral
A1: correct comparison/justification of which is more efficient
A1: correct final numeric area computed using the chosen setup
